info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 4.2: Layout Analysis and HTR Model Training in Transkribus.

name.text: 01 Question: What Deterministic Means This Week

questiontext.text: In what sense is a specialized HTR model 'deterministic' compared to a generative vision-language model?

generalfeedback.text: A specialized HTR model is bounded by its training data, which makes it fail rather than fabricate — the opposite of Friday's tools.

answer.text: It consistently produces identical output for the same input and is strictly bounded by its training data, reading visual character patterns rather than inventing plausible prose from linguistic expectations.

feedback.text: Correct. Specialized HTR fails on unseen hands rather than hallucinating plausible sentences from outside its training distribution.

answer.text: It relies entirely on hand-written if-then rules rather than statistical neural networks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. HTR uses learned neural networks, but its competence is strictly bounded by training data without generative linguistic completion.

answer.text: It can only transcribe printed typography and fails on all forms of cursive handwriting.

feedback.text: Incorrect. HTR is specifically designed for handwritten text.

answer.text: It guarantees 0% character error rate on every historical manuscript regardless of date.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Error rates depend on data quality and hand match; its boundedness means it fails rather than fabricates.

name.text: 02 Question: The Pipeline: Layout Before Recognition

questiontext.text: Why is document layout analysis strictly separated from character recognition in the HTR pipeline?

generalfeedback.text: Recognition only ever sees line images that layout analysis produced — so when output is bad, inspect the line images first.

answer.text: The recognition engine never sees the full page; it only transcribes line images produced by layout analysis, so spatial segmentation errors cascade directly into recognition failures.

feedback.text: Correct. If layout analysis merges, splits, or truncates a line image, no recognition model can recover the correct text.

answer.text: Layout analysis is performed on GPU clusters while recognition must be executed on quantum processors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both stages run on standard compute hardware; the separation is functional and sequential.

answer.text: The TEI XML specification prohibits software from analyzing typography and coordinates in the same pass.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI is an encoding standard, not an HTR pipeline execution constraint.

answer.text: Layout analysis determines the grammatical syntax of the text before the recognizer identifies letterforms.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Layout analysis detects physical regions and baselines; it has no grammatical knowledge.

name.text: 03 Question: From Bounding Boxes to Baselines

questiontext.text: Why do modern HTR systems use baseline detection and polygonal envelopes rather than rectangular bounding boxes for manuscript layout analysis?

generalfeedback.text: Modern layout analysis predicts sloping baselines and computes envelopes around them, because manuscript lines do not fit rectangles.

answer.text: Manuscript lines frequently slope, curve, and interleave with marginalia or interlinear additions, which cannot be captured accurately by rigid rectangular boxes.

feedback.text: Correct. Baselines follow the actual course of writing, and polygonal envelopes enclose ascenders and descenders without clipping adjacent lines.

answer.text: Rectangular bounding boxes require three times more GPU memory to calculate than polygonal meshes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Bounding boxes are computationally simpler, but they fail geometrically on irregular manuscript lines.

answer.text: Baselines allow the OCR engine to automatically translate Greek text into Latin.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Baselines provide geometric coordinates for line segmentation; they do not perform linguistic translation.

answer.text: International archival standards reject image scans that contain rectangular coordinates.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Standards support bounding boxes, but baselines are technically superior for historical layout.

questiontext.text: Why is importing manuscript images via a IIIF manifest URI preferable to uploading detached local image files into Transkribus?

generalfeedback.text: Import by manifest URI so training data stays linked to the institutional source rather than becoming a detached copy.

answer.text: It maintains the institutional provenance chain and links training data directly to the official high-resolution repository without creating unmanaged local copies.

feedback.text: Correct. Ingesting by manifest URI preserves image coordinates and provenance back to the institutional digital repository.

answer.text: IIIF manifests automatically perform Greek-to-English translation upon upload.

feedback.text: Incorrect. IIIF is an image delivery framework, not a machine translation tool.

answer.text: Local file uploads are charged double the credit rate per page compared to manifest imports.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Platform pricing is based on processed pages or units, not image ingest protocol.

answer.text: Transkribus prohibits all direct file uploads of JPEG and TIFF images.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Direct uploads are possible, but manifest imports preserve institutional linkage and reproducibility.

name.text: 05 Question: Running and Reading Layout Analysis

questiontext.text: When inspecting automated layout analysis results on Byzantine Greek manuscripts, what specific visual flaw must you look for in polygon envelopes?

generalfeedback.text: Check whether polygons enclose high-placed breathings and accents — if they do not, the model is being trained on Greek with the diacritics cut off.

answer.text: Whether the upper boundary of the polygon cuts off high-placed breathings, accents, or superscript abbreviations above the baseline.

feedback.text: Correct. High-placed diacritics falling outside the polygon boundary are excluded from the line image and lost to the recognizer.

answer.text: Whether the baseline polygon uses an odd number of vertices, which causes memory leaks in PyLaia.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Polygon vertex count does not cause PyLaia memory leaks; the issue is diacritic clipping.

answer.text: Whether the layout analyzer inverted the colour palette of the parchment.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Layout analysis identifies text coordinates, not image colour inversion.

answer.text: Whether the bounding polygon extends across the binding gutter into the opposite quire.

feedback.text: Incorrect. While region detection can err, the specific Greek hazard is diacritic truncation.

questiontext.text: What is an efficient strategy for correcting systematic layout polygon truncation across multiple pages of a single scribal hand?

generalfeedback.text: Adjust the layout parameters from a measurement of this hand rather than correcting page by page — and verify by looking at extracted line images.

answer.text: Measure the required vertical margin on one page, adjust the global layout analysis parameters accordingly, and re-run rather than manually editing every line polygon.

feedback.text: Correct. Setting global parameters based on empirical hand measurements addresses the root cause across all folios rapidly.

answer.text: Delete all baselines and allow the HTR recognition model to process the full page unsegmented.

feedback.text: Incorrect. HTR models require segmented line images; unsegmented pages cannot be recognized by line models.

answer.text: Scale down image resolution by 50% so that all accents fit inside standard bounding boxes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Downsampling destroys resolution and impairs character recognition.

answer.text: Shift the baseline down to the bottom of the page and let the system guess line intervals.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Drifting baselines cause severe recognition errors.

name.text: 07 Question: Aligning Your Ground Truth to Lines

questiontext.text: What is the danger of using automated line-text alignment when the transcription line count does not match the detected baseline count?

generalfeedback.text: Verify line alignment by spot-checking image against text — an off-by-one misalignment produces a model that has learned the wrong pairing entirely.

answer.text: A split or missed line creates an off-by-one error, systematically pairing every subsequent image with the wrong line's text and training the model on completely false associations.

feedback.text: Correct. Systematic off-by-one misalignment causes the neural network to learn the wrong text for every line image, producing fluent nonsense.

answer.text: The Transkribus server will permanently delete the uploaded ground truth file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The system will not delete files, but the training alignment will be systematically corrupted.

answer.text: The alignment algorithm will automatically inject Latin translations into the Greek transcription.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Alignment pairs existing strings to line zones without translating.

answer.text: The XML document will lose its RelaxNG schema declaration during synchronization.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Alignment affects line-image pairings in the platform, not local schema declarations.

name.text: 08 Question: How Recognition Works: CRNN and CTC

questiontext.text: Why does Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) make manual diplomatic transcription directly usable as training data without character-level bounding boxes?

generalfeedback.text: CTC training needs only line images paired with line text, which is why your diplomatic transcription is directly usable as training data.

answer.text: CTC is alignment-free; it computes the probability of the target character sequence summed over all possible alignments between visual image slices and characters.

feedback.text: Correct. CTC requires only paired line images and line text, eliminating the need to annotate the precise pixel coordinates of individual letters.

answer.text: CTC uses a built-in Greek dictionary to automatically look up word definitions and correct spelling errors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CTC is a loss function for sequence mapping without lexical dictionaries.

answer.text: CTC converts line images into vector fonts before running recurrent LSTM passes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CNN layers extract visual feature maps directly from raster line images.

answer.text: CTC requires human editors to manually label every ascender and descender in the image.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CTC eliminates the need for character-level manual alignment.

name.text: 09 Question: The Error Profile of a CTC Model

questiontext.text: Why is the characteristic failure mode of a CRNN-CTC model (like PyLaia) advantageous for scholarly post-correction?

generalfeedback.text: A CTC model's errors are conspicuous because it produces impossible sequences rather than plausible wrong words — which makes post-correction far more reliable.

answer.text: It produces conspicuous, orthographically impossible letter sequences when uncertain, making errors immediately obvious rather than disguising them as plausible wrong words.

feedback.text: Correct. A conspicuous error like ἐγενθτο is easily spotted, whereas a plausible wrong word like ἐγένετο for ἐγένοντο can easily slip past an editor.

answer.text: It automatically corrects scribal errors to match modern standard editions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Silent modernization is a liability; CTC models read visual ink rather than modernizing.

answer.text: It highlights all mistakes in red ink directly on the original manuscript facsimile.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CTC models output text strings; they do not alter source images.

answer.text: It achieves a 0% character error rate on all abbreviations and ligatures.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CTC models struggle on dense ligatures and abbreviations where character boundaries overlap.

questiontext.text: What is the trade-off when using a Transformer-based architecture like TrOCR instead of a CRNN-CTC model?

generalfeedback.text: Transformers read context as well as ink, which helps on degraded text and produces plausible wrong words that are hard to catch.

answer.text: TrOCR handles degraded text and complex layout better through strong global contextual modelling, but has a higher risk of hallucinating plausible wrong words that are hard to detect.

feedback.text: Correct. Autoregressive language modelling in the decoder drives the model toward plausible completions that may not match the actual ink.

answer.text: TrOCR is computationally cheaper and runs ten times faster on low-end CPUs than PyLaia.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transformer models are computationally heavier and require more resources.

answer.text: TrOCR completely eliminates the need for training data by generating transcriptions from zero-shot prompts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TrOCR models are supervised OCR architectures that require training or fine-tuning.

answer.text: TrOCR cannot process image files larger than 100 kilobytes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TrOCR processes standard image patch embeddings regardless of file size.

name.text: 11 Question: Transfer Learning: Never Start From Scratch

questiontext.text: What empirical evidence demonstrates the value of transfer learning in historical HTR model training?

generalfeedback.text: Transfer learning turned 17.18% CER into 3.90% on identical data — always fine-tune from a base model rather than training from scratch.

answer.text: Fine-tuning a pre-trained base model on multi-manuscript Byzantine Greek data reduced CER from 17.18% (from scratch) to 3.90% on identical data.

feedback.text: Correct. Starting from a pre-trained base model leverages learned features, delivering a fourfold improvement and reducing required ground truth by up to 80%.

answer.text: Training from scratch produces identical error rates but consumes 90% fewer compute credits.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Training from scratch produces vastly worse error rates and consumes far more compute.

answer.text: Transfer learning allows models trained on Chinese woodblocks to transcribe Greek uncials with 0% CER.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transfer learning requires a relevant domain base; cross-script transfer between unrelated scripts is ineffective.

answer.text: Starting from scratch is required by TEI guidelines to ensure independent data licensing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI guidelines do not mandate random weight initialization in neural networks.

questiontext.text: When selecting a base model for fine-tuning, which criterion is most critical for success on historical manuscripts?

generalfeedback.text: A matched small model beats a large general one — script match matters more than parameter count.

answer.text: Script and period match; a smaller model trained on the same script family vastly outperforms a massive general-purpose model.

feedback.text: Correct. Parameter scale cannot compensate for lack of exposure to specific palaeographical scripts, ligatures, and abbreviations.

answer.text: The total parameter count of the model, prioritizing models with over 70 billion parameters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. General massive models exhibit large specialization gaps on historical scripts.

answer.text: Whether the base model was trained exclusively on modern printed newspapers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Modern print models perform poorly on historical manuscript hands.

answer.text: The commercial market valuation of the company hosting the model API.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Domain palaeographical match is the decisive scholarly and empirical criterion.

questiontext.text: Why must you hold out a representative validation set during HTR model training, and when should training stop?

generalfeedback.text: Hold out a representative validation set and stop when validation error stops falling — a rising validation curve means the model is memorizing your lines.

answer.text: To measure performance on unseen lines and detect overfitting; training should stop when validation error reaches its minimum and begins to rise.

feedback.text: Correct. A rising validation loss indicates the model is memorizing specific training lines rather than generalizing to the hand.

answer.text: The validation set is sent to the TEI Consortium for remote accreditation; training stops after exactly 1000 epochs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Validation sets are local holdouts used to monitor generalization.

answer.text: To provide training data for the subsequent epoch; training stops when training loss reaches exactly zero.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Validation data is held out from training; stopping at zero training loss causes severe overfitting.

answer.text: To reduce Transkribus credit consumption by 50%; training stops when the GPU temperature exceeds 80°C.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Validation evaluates generalization and prevents overfitting.

questiontext.text: What is the practical threshold above which an HTR model's output is generally considered a net loss in scholarly workflow?

generalfeedback.text: Above 15% CER, correcting the output costs more than transcribing from scratch — the model is a net loss, not a slow tool.

answer.text: A CER over 15%, because the cognitive effort and time needed to post-correct errors exceeds the time required to transcribe manually from scratch.

feedback.text: Correct. Above 15% CER, human post-editing is slower and more error-prone than manual diplomatic transcription.

answer.text: A CER over 1%, because any digital edition with errors is automatically rejected by journals.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A 5–10% CER is good and usable for post-correction; 15% is the threshold of economic unviability.

answer.text: A WER over 50% on texts written in scriptio continua.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scriptio continua inflates WER artificially due to token segmentation without making character recognition useless.

answer.text: When validation CER is lower than training CER.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Validation CER is normally slightly higher than training CER, but this does not indicate workflow loss.

name.text: 15 Question: Error Rates Do Not Tell You Everything

questiontext.text: Why is Character Error Rate (CER) alone insufficient for evaluating the scholarly quality of an HTR transcription?

generalfeedback.text: CER weights every difference equally, so a model that silently drops diacritics or expands abbreviations can score well while being useless for a diplomatic edition.

answer.text: CER weights every character edit equally, so a model that silently drops diacritics or expands abbreviations can achieve a low CER while destroying diplomatic fidelity.

feedback.text: Correct. A low CER can mask systematic philological corruption such as silent normalization or lost breathings.

answer.text: CER only measures punctuation and completely ignores vowels and consonants.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CER measures all character insertions, deletions, and substitutions equally.

answer.text: CER cannot be calculated mathematically on non-English text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Levenshtein distance applies to any Unicode character sequence.

answer.text: CER calculations require access to the physical parchment in person.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CER is computed digitally between reference and hypothesis text strings.

name.text: 16 Question: Applying the Model and Inspecting the Output

questiontext.text: When an HTR model produces complete nonsense on a single line of an otherwise accurate page, what is the most likely cause?

generalfeedback.text: Categorize errors rather than just correcting them, and inspect the line image whenever output is nonsense — it is usually a layout fault.

answer.text: A layout analysis fault, such as a drifted baseline, a merged line, or a clipped polygon envelope.

feedback.text: Correct. Line-level catastrophic failure is almost always caused by a defective line image produced during layout segmentation.

answer.text: A sudden drop in internet connection speed during neural network inference.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Inference on an image slice is deterministic; network speed affects upload time, not inference logic.

answer.text: An overflow in the TEI RelaxNG validator memory cache.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI validation occurs after export, not during model inference.

answer.text: The scribe switching from ancient Greek to medieval Latin for that single line.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Layout errors are the standard cause of isolated line nonsense.

questiontext.text: What danger arises in the iterative HTR loop (correct output, add to training, retrain), and how is it broken?

generalfeedback.text: Each iteration makes ground truth cheaper, but correcting model output risks a feedback loop — periodically transcribe a page blind to break it.

answer.text: Editors may carelessly accept plausible model errors, causing the model to learn and amplify those errors in a feedback loop; broken by periodically transcribing a page blind.

feedback.text: Correct. Transcribing an occasional page from scratch without seeing model output breaks confirmation bias and feedback loops.

answer.text: The model's weights permanently lock after the second iteration, preventing further updates.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Retraining fine-tunes weights across all accumulated training data.

answer.text: Iterative retraining increases the character error rate exponentially on every pass.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Iterative retraining typically lowers CER if corrections are accurate.

answer.text: Transkribus restricts users to a single training iteration per collection.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The platform fully supports multi-pass iterative training workflows.

questiontext.text: Why did Geelhaar's Carolingian Minuscule Model degrade from 5.1% CER on standard pages to 13.6% on glossed pages?

generalfeedback.text: A model's CER holds only for layouts like those it was validated on — glossed or irregular pages need their own measurement.

answer.text: The model was brittle to layout shifts; smaller marginal glosses introduced shifting vocabulary, heavier abbreviations, and reduced visual resolution.

feedback.text: Correct. HTR models are conditioned on layout topography; performance degrades when encountering irregular formatting outside training data.

answer.text: The glosses were written in twentieth-century ballpoint pen ink.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The glosses were historical medieval additions in minuscule script.

answer.text: The Transkribus server crashed during the processing of marginal columns.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The degradation was an empirical recognition failure due to layout complexity.

answer.text: Marginal glosses violate XML well-formedness rules during OCR processing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Layout brittleness is a computer vision and domain variance issue, not an XML syntax error.

questiontext.text: What is the core methodological trade-off between Transkribus and eScriptorium for digital scholarly editing?

generalfeedback.text: Transkribus is more accessible; eScriptorium is reproducible — and a proprietary model makes any claim resting on it unverifiable later.

answer.text: Transkribus offers an accessible graphical interface and a large public model library, while eScriptorium provides complete open-source transparency and long-term reproducibility.

feedback.text: Correct. Proprietary commercial models may become unavailable over time, whereas open models and engines can be archived and verified indefinitely.

answer.text: Transkribus only works on legacy operating systems, while eScriptorium requires a supercomputer.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both have modern web or desktop access; the difference is licensing and open architecture.

answer.text: eScriptorium does not support baseline detection and relies exclusively on rectangular bounding boxes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. eScriptorium uses Kraken with YALTAi for advanced baseline detection.

answer.text: Transkribus exports only proprietary binary blobs that cannot be converted to XML.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transkribus exports standard PAGE XML, ALTO XML, and TEI.

name.text: 20 Question: Exporting: PAGE, ALTO, and TEI

questiontext.text: How can exported ALTO XML coordinates be used to accelerate the creation of TEI <surface> and <zone> elements?

generalfeedback.text: ALTO preserves line coordinates in image pixels — transform them into TEI zones and check the result against your hand-measured control lines.

answer.text: ALTO's <TextLine> pixel coordinates can be transformed into TEI <zone> elements automatically, verified against hand-measured control lines.

feedback.text: Correct. Transforming ALTO coordinates scales line bounding boxes into TEI zones across the entire document, replacing manual coordinate measurement.

answer.text: ALTO XML coordinates automatically replace all polytonic Greek characters with Unicode control characters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. ALTO stores text strings and spatial coordinates without altering Unicode integrity.

answer.text: ALTO XML cannot be converted into TEI without purchasing a proprietary commercial compiler.

feedback.text: Incorrect. ALTO is an open XML format that can be transformed via standard scripts or stylesheets.

answer.text: The coordinates in ALTO XML represent physical millimeters on the parchment rather than image pixels.

feedback.text: Incorrect. ALTO coordinates are in image pixel space, which must be mapped to TEI facsimile coordinates.

questiontext.text: Why must raw HTR model output and subsequent human corrections be committed in separate Git commits?

generalfeedback.text: Commit raw model output and your corrections separately, or Week 5 cannot compute an error rate at all.

answer.text: To preserve the exact uncorrected machine state for objective error rate measurement in Week 5, while documenting clear provenance trailers.

feedback.text: Correct. Committing raw output separately allows scoring against ground truth and maintains an audit trail with Human-Verified: false.

answer.text: Git refuses to commit any file that contains both human and machine-generated lines.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git is content-agnostic and commits any text provided in the staging area.

answer.text: Separate commits are required to trigger automated billing refunds on Transkribus.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git commits have no connection to platform financial billing.

answer.text: Merging them into a single commit causes the pre-commit NFC normalization hook to delete the file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The hook normalizes Unicode characters; it does not block single commits.

name.text: 22 Question: What Today Establishes for Friday

questiontext.text: When comparing today's specialized HTR model with Friday's vision-language model, why must you record cost (time and effort) alongside error rates?

generalfeedback.text: Record cost as well as quality — Friday's tool needs no training or ground truth, and the comparison is meaningless without that.

answer.text: Friday's zero-shot model requires no ground truth or training time, so an honest methodological evaluation must weigh setup investment against output quality.

feedback.text: Correct. A tool that takes 5 minutes with higher error may be preferable for some tasks than one requiring 10 hours of setup for low error, and vice versa.

answer.text: Tracking time is required to calculate the electrical kilowatt consumption of the campus computer lab.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tracking time measures human and computational workflow costs for scholarly method evaluation.

answer.text: Vision-language models bill users per second of human reading time.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Commercial APIs bill per token or image, not human reading duration.

answer.text: Time tracking is used to automatically adjust the learning rate of Friday's model.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Friday uses pre-trained zero-shot models whose architecture is fixed.

name.text: 23 Question: Why the Specialized Model Usually Wins

questiontext.text: What is the 'specialization gap' observed when applying large vision-language models to historical handwriting?

generalfeedback.text: General models are excellent on modern handwriting and catastrophic on historical scripts — scale does not substitute for exposure to the material.

answer.text: General models excel on modern handwriting (e.g. GPT-4o at 1.39% CER) but fail severely on historical scripts (over 50% CER), where smaller domain-tuned models succeed due to direct palaeographical exposure.

feedback.text: Correct. Internet-scale training data contains vast modern text but minimal historical minuscule, so scale does not compensate for lack of domain exposure.

answer.text: Vision-language models refuse to process images of historical documents due to safety guardrails.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Models process the images willingly, but lack the domain-specific feature representations needed for accurate transcription.

answer.text: Specialized models have 100 times more parameters than commercial vision-language models.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Specialized HTR models have millions of parameters, whereas VLMs have billions.

answer.text: The gap is caused by vision-language models being unable to process RGB colour channels.

feedback.text: Incorrect. VLMs process high-resolution colour images natively.

questiontext.text: What happens when an LLM post-correction stage is added to an OCR or HTR pipeline on historical manuscripts?

generalfeedback.text: Adding LLM post-correction to OCR degrades quality — it corrects toward plausibility, and unusual readings are the interesting ones.

answer.text: It degrades aggregate accuracy because the LLM has no access to the image and alters correct unusual readings into plausible common words, propagating cascading errors.

feedback.text: Correct. Empirical studies show simpler direct pipelines outperform complex RAG or LLM post-correction chains on historical text.

answer.text: It accelerates processing speed by converting character images into vector embeddings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Additional pipeline stages increase latency and computational overhead.

answer.text: It completely eliminates all character substitution errors without altering word boundaries.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Generative post-correction introduces temporal hallucinations and modernizations.

answer.text: It automatically converts Greek polytonic accents into TEI XML tags.

feedback.text: Incorrect. LLM post-correction modifies text strings and tends to normalize historical variants.

questiontext.text: What should you do if your trained HTR model yields a validation CER exceeding 15%?

generalfeedback.text: If validation CER exceeds 15%, diagnose rather than correct — check layout, then alignment, then data volume, then base model.

answer.text: Diagnose root causes systematically (layout errors, ground truth misalignment, data volume, base model match) rather than spending hours correcting the output.

feedback.text: Correct. Above 15% CER, post-correction is slower than manual transcription; the model must be diagnosed and retrained.

answer.text: Immediately delete the repository and restart the entire course from Lesson 1.1.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Systematic diagnosis of layout, alignment, or base model usually resolves high CER.

answer.text: Manually edit all the validation predictions to read 0% error in the log file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Falsifying validation logs defeats the purpose of empirical measurement.

answer.text: Pass the output through three successive LLM filters to correct the spelling.

feedback.text: Incorrect. As established in section 24, LLM post-correction degrades historical transcription quality.

questiontext.text: When HTR output is unexpectedly inaccurate in a way you cannot explain, what is the single most effective diagnostic action?

generalfeedback.text: When output is inexplicably wrong, look at the extracted line image — that is what the model actually saw.

answer.text: Inspect the extracted line image to see exactly what visual data the recognition model actually received.

feedback.text: Correct. Almost every inexplicable recognition failure stems from a truncated polygon, drifted baseline, or misaligned image slice.

answer.text: Increase the number of epochs to 10,000 and run training overnight.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Over-training on bad input data amplifies errors and causes severe overfitting.

answer.text: Switch your computer's operating system language to modern Greek.

feedback.text: Incorrect. OS localization has no impact on server-side HTR inference.

answer.text: Re-install Python and delete all Git commit trailers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The issue lies in the input image data fed to the neural network.

questiontext.text: Why is a reported CER figure (e.g. '6.2% CER') scientifically meaningless without an accompanying methodology record?

generalfeedback.text: A CER figure is uninterpretable without its base model, training volume, and validation set — record the methodology today.

answer.text: CER is conditional; without knowing the base model, training volume, layout adjustments, and validation set composition, the number cannot be interpreted or reproduced.

feedback.text: Correct. Documenting parameters and data splits in logs/htr-method-w4.md is what turns raw numbers into reproducible scholarly findings.

answer.text: The number is invalid unless accompanied by a certified receipt from Transkribus billing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scientific validity depends on methodological transparency, not commercial receipts.

answer.text: CER can only be reported if it was calculated using proprietary closed-source benchmark suites.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CER is standard Levenshtein distance, but its meaning depends on experimental context.

answer.text: Any CER below 10% is automatically rejected by journals unless proven by a mathematical lemma.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Clear documentation of data, models, and validation splits is the standard requirement.

questiontext.text: Why must you have Git tags for both the manual ground truth (gt-f42r) and raw HTR output (htr-w4-raw) before Friday's remote session?

generalfeedback.text: Tag all three states so Friday's three-way comparison is exact, and expect the general model to be much worse and much faster.

answer.text: To enable an exact, reproducible three-way comparison on identical lines across all three states during Friday's analysis.

feedback.text: Correct. Tags ensure you can extract the exact snapshots needed for line-by-line comparison and diff analysis.

answer.text: Friday's vision-language model cannot connect to GitHub unless repository tags are public.

feedback.text: Incorrect. VLMs process images and prompts independently of Git tags.

answer.text: Tagging files automatically converts Transkribus XML exports into markdown tables.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git tags are reference pointers; format transformation is handled by scripts.

answer.text: Without Git tags, remote clones will permanently lose all commit history.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Commits remain on branches, but tags provide exact scholarly handles for comparison.

name.text: 29 Question: What Good Work Looks Like Here

questiontext.text: What distinguishes a high-quality scholarly evaluation of an HTR model from mere tool operation?

generalfeedback.text: Reporting what the model gets wrong and why is the scholarly contribution; the CER number alone is tool operation.

answer.text: Analyzing what the model gets wrong (error categorization, layout vs. recognition failures) and explaining the palaeographical and architectural reasons why.

feedback.text: Correct. The scholarly contribution lies in qualitative diagnosis and understanding system limits, not just reporting an aggregate error number.

answer.text: Achieving 0.00% CER by training on the validation set itself.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Evaluating on training data is a methodological fallacy that invalidates measurement.

answer.text: Generating over 10,000 pages of uninspected machine transcription in one afternoon.

feedback.text: Incorrect. High volume without validation is uncritical tool operation.

answer.text: Writing custom C++ CUDA kernels to rewrite the PyLaia engine from scratch.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly evaluation focuses on critical analysis of results against historical evidence.

questiontext.text: What is the fundamental operational difference between Wednesday's specialized HTR model and Friday's vision-language model?

generalfeedback.text: An HTR model reads ink within the bounds of its training and fails conspicuously; Friday's instrument reads expectation too, and fails fluently.

answer.text: The HTR model is a bounded instrument that reads ink within its training distribution and fails conspicuously, while the VLM is an unbounded model that applies linguistic expectation and fails fluently.

feedback.text: Correct. Bounded models produce obvious letter errors; unbounded generative models fabricate plausible prose that disguises transcription failure.

answer.text: The HTR model is entirely open-source and free, while vision-language models can only be run on local mainframes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both have various commercial or open hosting models; the difference is architecture and failure modes.

answer.text: The HTR model requires internet access during inference, while vision-language models run entirely on paper.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both are software systems; the contrast is bounded recognition versus generative completion.

answer.text: The HTR model cannot process Greek, while the vision-language model cannot process English.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both can process multiple languages, but their failure profiles differ drastically on historical hands.
